title: Incident remediation SLAs vs Contract SLAs — customer comms alignment (draft v0.7)
body:
Context / why this doc exists
- We are standardizing Incident Taxonomy v1 + internal remediation SLAs (TTM/TTR) so that Eng/SRE can be consistent and we can measure MTTR.
- In parallel, Support/CS needs customer-facing language that does NOT accidentally promise contractual terms (or conflict with existing MSA/SOW uptime SLAs), but still provides clear expectations during an active incident.
- This is a working draft for alignment across Product, CS, and SRE. Not a legal doc.

Audience
- Primary: Customer Success, Support, Incident Comms (Jasmine/Rachel/Dev)
- Secondary: SRE ICs / incident commanders (Sean/Rafael), Product (Marissa/Lauren)

Status
- v0.7 (draft). Needs sign-off from Rachel (enterprise comms) + Sean (SRE) + Marissa/Lauren (product).
- Next: fold into Confluence playbook + incident-bot canned messages.

Definitions (important)
1) Contract SLA (a/k/a uptime SLA)
- Customer contract language usually defines monthly availability target(s), service credits, measurement method, exclusions.
- Contract SLA is evaluated post-incident, typically over a billing month and may exclude scheduled maintenance, customer-side network issues, force majeure, etc.
- Contract SLA is NOT the same thing as “how fast we respond” or “how quickly we restore.”

2) Remediation SLA (internal operational target)
- Internal targets for:
  - TTM (time to mitigate): time until impact is stopped or materially reduced (e.g., rollback, failover, disable feature flag, shift traffic).
  - TTR (time to resolution / permanent fix): time until root cause is fixed or durable mitigation is in place, with follow-ups tracked via action items.
- These are operational commitments we aim to meet; they are not currently contractually guaranteed unless explicitly stated in an enterprise SOW.

3) “Customer-facing ETA”
- An estimate for next update time (not fix time) or for mitigation steps.
- We should prefer “next update at <time>” over “fixed by <time>” unless SRE explicitly confirms.

4) Severity
- Use existing incident severity definitions (Sev1/Sev2/Sev3). This doc does not redefine severity.
- Severity should drive comms cadence and who is paged.

Core principle: separate three things in customer communications
A) Operational status: what is impacted, who is impacted, since when, current behavior, workarounds.
B) Internal targets: “we are actively working; next update by…” and optionally “we are prioritizing mitigation.”
C) Contractual SLA: only discuss after-the-fact when we have data and the contract terms in front of us.

What we are aligning to (taxonomy + remediation SLAs)
- Engineering is publishing a remediation mapping by (severity x incident category x tier), e.g. routing failures, capacity exhaustion, runtime crash, etc.
- CS/Support should not quote internal category names unless helpful and non-confusing. We can describe in plain language and optionally map to “control plane/routing” vs “capacity” etc.

Product surfaces / tiers (customer-facing)
- Hosted API (self-serve)
- Dedicated Capacity (reserved pools; enterprise)
- Private (VPC/on-prem where Redwood is primary operator for day-2 ops)

Comms channels
- Hosted API: status page + support tickets (and enterprise Slack Connect where applicable)
- Dedicated/Private: named customer channel (Slack Connect / email distro) + ticket + status page if broad impact

What we can safely say (approved language patterns)
1) Response acknowledgement
- “We’ve identified elevated error rates/timeouts affecting <surface> starting at <time> <timezone>. Our engineering team is actively investigating. Next update by <time>.”

2) Mitigation focus (without hard promises)
- “We are prioritizing mitigation steps to reduce customer impact (e.g., traffic shifting / rollback / capacity adjustments). We’ll share another update by <time> or sooner if conditions change.”

3) When asked: “What’s your SLA?” (during incident)
- “Our contracts define availability targets measured over the billing month. During an active incident, our focus is restoring service as quickly as possible; we’ll provide regular updates and we can review any SLA/credit implications after the incident with full data.”

4) If customer pushes for remediation target times
- “We track internal response and mitigation targets to drive reliability, but those are not contractual guarantees unless specified in your agreement. The best immediate signal we can provide is our next update time and current mitigation progress.”

5) For Dedicated/Private where we have stronger expectations (but still careful)
- “Given your tier, we are treating this as highest priority and have engaged the on-call SRE + service owner. Next update by <time>.”

6) Closing message
- “Service has returned to normal as of <time>. We’ll follow up with a written incident summary and next steps. If you’d like, we can schedule a review.”

Things we should not say (unless explicitly confirmed + approved)
- “We guarantee mitigation within X minutes.” (unless contract/SOW explicitly says so)
- “This counts toward SLA credits” during incident.
- “Root cause is <X>” before post-incident confirmation.
- “No data was impacted” unless Security/Eng confirms.
- “This will never happen again.”

Update cadence guidelines (draft; align with Support playbook)
Sev1 (material production impact)
- First customer-facing acknowledgement: within 15 minutes of incident declaration for enterprise channels; within 30 minutes for broad Hosted incidents if going to status page.
- Updates: every 30 minutes until mitigation; then hourly until fully resolved.
- Must include: current impact, what we’re doing, next update time.

Sev2 (degraded performance/partial impact)
- Acknowledge: within 30–60 minutes depending on tier and blast radius.
- Updates: every 60–120 minutes.

Sev3 (minor/localized)
- Acknowledge: within 1 business day unless enterprise escalation.

Note: cadence can be faster if the customer is blocked, but avoid high-frequency “no change” noise. Better to send a crisp “no change; next update at…”

How internal remediation SLAs relate to customer comms (practical rules)
- Internal TTM target should inform how aggressively we run the incident + escalation, but not necessarily be quoted.
- If we are on track, we can message confidence qualitatively (“we are actively mitigating”) without numbers.
- If we are off track (e.g., exceeded internal TTM), comms should become more explicit: acknowledge prolonged impact, state escalations engaged, and provide next update time.

Customer tier considerations
Hosted API (self-serve)
- Use status page for broad issues; use ticket responses for customer-specific issues.
- Avoid promising bespoke ETAs; use “next update” language.

Dedicated
- Customers expect stronger engagement: page the owning team + SRE, and provide higher-touch comms.
- If impact is limited to their pool/region, consider not posting publicly on status page; keep in private channel + ticket.

Private
- Clarify operator boundary up front:
  - If Redwood is primary operator (day-2 ops), we provide incident comms similar to Dedicated.
  - If customer operates the environment, provide best-effort guidance; avoid taking ownership for customer-controlled infra.

Common customer questions + suggested replies
Q: “Are we getting SLA credits?”
A: “We’ll review availability and contract terms after the incident with complete data. Right now we’re focused on restoring service and keeping you updated.”

Q: “What’s your MTTR / how fast do you fix this?”
A: “Resolution time varies by incident type. We run a formal incident process with continuous updates, and we’ll share a detailed incident summary afterward including timing and corrective actions.”

Q: “Is this a platform-wide issue or just us?”
A: “At this time we’re seeing impact in <region/surface>. We’re investigating scope and will update you by <time> with what we know.”

Q: “Is data exposed / security breach?”
A: “We have no indication of unauthorized access at this time. We’ll confirm through our investigation and will follow our security incident process if anything suggests a security event.”

Incident summary expectations (post-incident)
- For enterprise (Dedicated/Private) provide within 3–5 business days:
  - timeline (start, detect, mitigate, resolve)
  - customer impact description
  - root cause (plain language + technical appendix optional)
  - remediation actions (what we changed)
  - prevention/next steps (action items with owners)

Draft templates (copy/paste)

Template A — Initial acknowledgement (Sev1)
Subject: [Redwood] Investigating <errors/timeouts/degraded performance> impacting <Hosted API/Dedicated cluster/Private deployment>
Body:
- We are investigating elevated <5xx/timeouts/latency> affecting <surface> starting at <time>.
- Current impact: <who/what/region>.
- Current status: <investigating/mitigating/monitoring>.
- Next update: by <time>.

Template B — Mitigation in progress
- We have identified <suspected component/area> and are taking mitigation steps (e.g., <rollback/shift traffic/increase capacity>).
- We are monitoring for improvement. Next update by <time>.

Template C — Resolved
- The issue has been mitigated/resolved as of <time>.
- Current status: service operating normally.
- Next steps: we will provide a written incident summary and corrective actions. If you’d like a review call, we can schedule.

Open questions (needs alignment)
1) Do we want different comms cadences by tier (Dedicated vs Hosted) codified, or keep as guidelines?
2) Are there any existing SOWs that include response-time language that conflicts with this doc?
3) What is the official “status page threshold” for Dedicated-only incidents (post publicly vs private-only comms)?
4) Do we want a standard line referencing internal remediation targets at all (“we have internal targets”), or avoid entirely?

Action items / next steps
- Rachel: review templates for enterprise tone + consistency with existing customer comms. (due 2025-02-18)
- Jasmine + Dev: map templates into Support playbook by incident category and add “when to post to status page.”
- Aisha + Sean: confirm we are not contradicting the remediation SLA mapping language; provide any “must include” fields during active incident updates.
- Marissa/Lauren: confirm Dedicated contract patterns; flag any customers with bespoke language.

Notes to self (Marissa)
- Keep this doc intentionally conservative: we can always be more specific in 1:1 comms when SRE confirms, but we can’t take back accidental promises.
- Ensure the incident-bot “customer update” snippets align with this language (next update times, no contract credit talk).
